# 📖 Book — How to Take Smart Notes

> *Literature note.* Author: **Sönke Ahrens** (2017). Read Jan 2024, re-skimmed Feb 2026.
> Rating: ★★★★☆

A book about the *Zettelkasten* method of the sociologist Niklas Luhmann, who published
58 books and ~600 articles by treating note-taking as the primary work rather than a
chore that precedes the work.

## The one-sentence summary

Don't take notes *about* what you read; take notes that **argue with** what you read and
connect it to what you already think — then writing becomes a matter of arranging notes
you already wrote.[^slip]

## The note types Ahrens distinguishes

| Type | Lifespan | Purpose |
|------|----------|---------|
| Fleeting | Hours | Capture; throw away after processing |
| Literature | Permanent-ish | One per source, in your own words |
| Permanent | Forever | The atomic ideas — my [[Evergreen Notes]] |

This three-tier split maps almost exactly onto my seedling/budding/evergreen states from
[[On Tending a Digital Garden]], which is partly why the book clicked.

## What I took and what I left

**Took:**

- "Write to think, don't think to write." The blank page is not where ideas come from; the
  note collection is.
- The insistence on **atomicity**, which became the backbone of [[Evergreen Notes]].

**Left:**

- The fetishization of a single numbered ID scheme. Wikilinks like `[[Idempotency Is a
  Superpower]]` do the same job as Luhmann's `21/3a4` IDs without the bookkeeping. The
  *link*, not the *address*, is the unit that matters.

## A passage worth keeping

> "The slip-box is not a collection of notes. Working with it is less about retrieving
> specific notes and more about being pointed to relevant facts and generating insight by
> letting ideas mingle."

That "letting ideas mingle" is the entire reason [[Compost Is a Distributed System]]
exists — two unrelated notes touched in the box and reacted.

## See also

- [[Evergreen Notes]]
- [[On Tending a Digital Garden]]

[^slip]: Luhmann called his system a *Zettelkasten* — literally "slip-box," a box of paper
slips. The physical constraint (one idea per slip) is what forced atomicity. Software
removes the constraint, so we have to impose it on ourselves.
